h1:
Paknampho Chinese Food
Dim Sum, Khao Tom Kui & Old-School Spots
intro: Paknampho is the real Chinese town of the Chao Phraya basin. Five dialect groups — Teochew, Hokkien, Hakka, Hainanese and Cantonese — put down roots at the river junction back in the late reign of Rama V, and that heritage still lives on the plate today: hot dim sum in the morning, river fish in the old Chinese restaurants, and khao tom kui that runs late into the night. We've picked the places Nakhon Sawan locals actually eat at and laid them out for you.

blocks.html: To really get Paknampho, start at the table. This town was a hub for Chinese migrants who came to trade along the river, and each dialect group brought its own home recipes. After a hundred-odd years, that food became the taste of the town. People here eat dim sum for breakfast like it's the most normal thing in the world, they're known for clown knifefish and butter catfish pulled from the river, and they meet up at khao tom kui shops at night. We've arranged things by the rhythm of the day, starting with morning and working through to late night.

blocks.text: 8 Paknampho Chinese restaurants the locals go to

blocks.html: This list isn't ranked by which place is better than another — it's ordered by the time of day Nakhon Sawan locals actually eat there, from morning dim sum to big sit-down dinners to late-night rice soup. Just pick by the meal you're in the mood for.

items.name: Leng Hong Restaurant
items.blurb: An old Chinese restaurant that's been part of Paknampho for 40-50 years and the first name locals think of for a banquet or bringing relatives out for a big meal. The standouts are river fish like clown knifefish, steamed fish curry (haw mok) with mackerel, prawns in tamarind sauce, and honey-roasted duck — classic Chinese banquet flavours. It works well coming as a family or a group.

items.name: Morning dim sum around Paknampho Market
items.blurb: Dim sum here is the town's breakfast, not a fancy treat for special occasions. Shops around the old market start opening their hot steamer baskets before dawn — pork dumplings (khanom jeeb), har gow, steamed buns, braised chicken feet — eaten with congee or old-style coffee. With marble tabletops and a coffee-shop crowd, it's the clearest taste of the town's Chinese roots.
items.meta: Paknampho Market area · early morning to late morning

items.name: Somkuan Phochana (khao tom kui)
items.blurb: A well-known Thai-Chinese khao tom kui spot in Paknampho, with dishes laid out on trays for you to pick and eat alongside hot rice soup — high-heat stir-fried veggies, spicy catfish stir-fry, pork-bone soup (leng), clear soups, omelettes. It's known for fresh ingredients, generous portions and easy prices, and locals come as whole families in the evening.
items.meta: Sawanwithi Rd, behind Wisutsuksa School · evening to late night

items.name: Nai Chuea Rice Soup
items.blurb: A Thai-Chinese rice soup and made-to-order spot open from afternoon till late, good for anyone hungry in the evening or after work. The menu is big and the seasoning is bold and full-flavoured in the Chinese style, so it's easy to order a few dishes to go with your rice soup. It's another pin on the map for the late-night eaters around Sawanwithi Rd.

items.name: Kamonwan Rice Soup
items.blurb: A two-unit shophouse near Kasikornbank on Sawanwithi Rd, serving rice soup from evening till late. The menu is the familiar comfort lineup — jungle curry, sour curry, fluffy omelette — and two or three people can eat for under three hundred baht. It's a regular for locals around here who drop in out of habit.
items.meta: Sawanwithi Rd, near KBank · evening to late night

items.name: Na Pha Fried Fish & Fish Cakes
items.blurb: An old shop right by the Na Pha Chinese shrine on Kosi Rd, serving the kind of homely Thai-Chinese food they've cooked here for years. Fried fish, fish cakes and river-fish dishes are what they do best, and the spot next to the shrine makes it an easy lunch after you've paid your respects.
items.meta: Kosi Rd, next to Na Pha shrine · open 09:00–20:00

items.name: Late-night congee around Paknampho
items.blurb: This town is known for being able to find food almost 24 hours a day, and congee carts and shops along the main roads stay open late for the night owls. Minced-pork congee with a soft-boiled egg, braised offal, topped with shredded ginger and spring onion — hot and easy down the throat. It's the classic way Paknampho's Chinese close out the night.
items.meta: Main roads in town · late night

items.name: Wonton noodles & roast duck (old-timers)
items.blurb: Wonton noodles and Chinese-style rice topped with duck or red pork are scattered around the morning markets and the old commercial district. House-made noodles, broth simmered from bones, crispy-skinned roast duck with a rich sauce — a light meal that fills you up just right, perfect for a market stroll.
items.meta: Morning markets / old commercial district · morning to afternoon

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.html: A lot of the dim sum and old-school noodle places sell out before noon, while the khao tom kui spots come alive in the evening and run late. If you want both in one day, plan to eat dim sum first thing in the morning and save the rice soup for dinner.

blocks.text: Why Paknampho Chinese food is special

blocks.html: What sets this place apart is that Chinese food isn't reserved for special occasions — it's the everyday food of the whole town. Dim sum is breakfast, river fish is the local pride, and khao tom kui is where people meet up at night. Recipes handed down over generations give each shop its own accent: some lean Teochew, soft and sweet; others lean Cantonese, with a clear broth.

items: River fish — Paknampho sits at a river junction, so clown knifefish, butter catfish and giant gourami are the main ingredients of the Chinese restaurants here.
Dim sum as breakfast — not a luxury, but a morning meal paired with old-style coffee on a marble table.
Khao tom kui — dishes laid out on trays to eat with hot rice soup, the late-night eating culture of the town's Chinese community.
Open all day — Paknampho has food almost 24 hours a day, from morning dim sum to late-night congee.

blocks.text: How to eat your way through Paknampho's Chinese flavours

items.name: Dim sum breakfast
items.blurb: Start your day around Paknampho Market with pork dumplings, har gow and steamed buns alongside congee or old-style coffee, and soak up that morning Chinese-town atmosphere.

items.name: Big river-fish meal
items.blurb: Bring the family or a group to an old-school restaurant like Leng Hong and order clown knifefish, steamed fish curry and tamarind prawns to share around the table.

items.name: Late-night khao tom kui
items.blurb: Close out the night at a rice-soup shop around Sawanwithi Rd, scooping dishes off the tray to eat with hot rice soup, or slurp down a late-night bowl of congee.

blocks.title: Good to know
blocks.html: Many of the old-school shops are cash-only with limited seating. Things get especially busy around Chinese New Year, since Paknampho is one of Thailand's most famous Chinese New Year towns — allow extra time to wait and keep some cash on you to make life easier.

faq.q: What Paknampho Chinese food should I try?
faq.a: Morning dim sum around Paknampho Market, river fish like clown knifefish at an old Chinese restaurant such as Leng Hong, and khao tom kui from evening into the late night around Sawanwithi Rd. Those three flavours capture the Chinese character of the town better than anything.

faq.q: Which is the oldest Chinese restaurant in Nakhon Sawan?
faq.a: Leng Hong Restaurant on Phromnimit Rd has been part of Paknampho for 40-50 years and is popular for banquets and big group meals. It's known for river fish and Chinese banquet-style cooking, open daily 09:30–22:00.

faq.q: Where's the best khao tom kui in Paknampho?
faq.a: The well-known spot is Somkuan Phochana on Sawanwithi Rd, behind Wisutsuksa School, where dishes are laid out on trays to eat with rice soup. There's also Nai Chuea and Kamonwan on the same road, both open from evening till late.

faq.q: When should I eat Paknampho dim sum?
faq.a: Dim sum here is a breakfast thing. Shops in the old market start steaming baskets before dawn and usually sell out before noon, so go early to get everything hot and the full menu.

Yes. Paknampho is known for having food almost 24 hours a day. Beyond the khao tom kui spots around Sawanwithi Rd, there are congee carts and made-to-order shops open late along the main roads in town.
